fuseState renders FuseState.INHERIT (144) and any other byte as `byte N`. This only affects display: the comparison against ENABLE/DISABLE still raises a violation, so the check is not a silent fallback.

parseFuseWires walks every sentinel, where @electron/fuses' getCurrentFuseWire reads only the first. A cross-check test against getCurrentFuseWire and the stock-binary control together show the reader sees real wires.

fuseState (scripts/verify-packaged.ts) has no branch for FuseState.INHERIT (144), so it shows as 'byte 144'. This only affects the message: verifyFuses compares the byte strictly to ENABLE/DISABLE, so an INHERIT byte is still reported as a violation.

The code deep-imports @electron/fuses/dist/constants.js. That works because the package has no exports map and the version is pinned at exactly 1.8.0, as the comment says; upgrading the package could break it.
On darwin, fuseBinaryPath takes the first path segment ending in .app. If a parent directory's name ended in .app, it would pick the wrong bundle. That is unlikely for out/ build paths.

scripts/repo-settings.ts tagRulesetGaps(): the single bypass actor's bypass_mode is never checked. Only actor_type and actor_id are compared, so the check accepts RepositoryRole 5 with any bypass mode.

The ruleset list and the deployment-branch-policies list read one page each (per_page=100) and do not paginate. That fails closed for rulesets (a missed ruleset means a violation, not a pass), and both counts are far below 100 in practice.
policyKey treats a missing policy type as 'branch'. That matches the API's default, and with it a missing type cannot pass as the required tag policy.

scripts/repo-settings.ts collect(): the final catch-all returns 'the settings check failed unexpectedly' and drops the error entirely. It fails closed and is commented, but a malformed API body (e.g. deployment_branch_policy missing, branch_policies absent, ruleset list not an array) gives an operator no hint which endpoint or field broke. Logging the error name or the last path read would help without risking the token.

scripts/repo-settings.ts evaluate(): only one compliant covering ruleset is needed for the rules, enforcement and bypass checks, yet the exclude check flags every covering ruleset. A non-compliant draft ruleset that excludes refs/tags/* would fail the check even when another active ruleset holds. This errs toward failing, but it is inconsistent with the 'a second, compliant tag ruleset is enough' test.
The rulesets and deployment-branch-policies lists are read with per_page=100 and no pagination. That is fine at this repo's scale, and anything past page one only makes the check fail.

verify-macos unpacks the whole signed dist-packaged tree (tar -C dist-packaged .) and runs layout --mode release on it. Whether sign-mac.ts's output matches the layout the old package:desktop --sign produced can only be confirmed on a real tag run.

release-workflow.spec pins job order, needs, environment confinement, tar hand-off, fuses-before-upload per release path and the trap-before-decode order. The policy spec covers each forbidden command both as its own step and inside the sign step.

The secret-job allowlist in scripts/workflow-policy.ts (PLAIN_SHELL plus the tar rule in allowedInSecretJob) lets a job overwrite the code it then runs. Allowed commands can redirect to any file, e.g. `echo ... > scripts/sign-mac.ts` or `base64 --decode > signing/package.json`, and `tar -xf x.tar` with no -C extracts into the checkout. A later allowed `node scripts/sign-mac.ts` or signing install then runs whatever was written. The shipped release.yml does neither, but ci:policy would not catch a workflow edit that did. Consider refusing redirections and tar extraction into scripts/, signing/ or the workspace root.

checkP8Cleanup only inspects `run:` keys under a block-style step (`- run:`). A .p8 write in a flow-style step (`- { run: ... }`) in a job without secrets is not checked. In a secret-bearing job the same step is already refused as unclassifiable.
